turns.text: I need a Python function `def rate_limit(requests: list, limit: int, global_limit: int, window: int) -> list` for an API rate limiter. Each request is a tuple `(timestamp, client_id)`; each client may make at most `limit` requests per `window` seconds, and all clients together at most `global_limit` per window. Return a list of booleans, one per request (True = accepted).

A couple of details: timestamps are integer seconds, the list is sorted by timestamp (non-decreasing), and requests are processed in list order. Also add a parameter `cooldown: int = 0` at the end. When a request from client c at time t is rejected by the limits, client c goes on cooldown: every later request from c with a timestamp strictly less than t + cooldown is rejected immediately, without any checks.

Let me pin down the limit checks. A request from client c at time t is accepted only if both pass: (a) fewer than `limit` of c's previously accepted requests have a timestamp in the half-open window `(t - window, t]`, and (b) fewer than `global_limit` of all clients' previously accepted requests have a timestamp in that same window. So a request exactly `window` seconds old has already dropped out. Only accepted requests count: rejected requests, for whatever reason, never count toward any later check.

Correction on the cooldown: I don't want every rejection to trigger it. Only a request that fails check (a), the client's own limit, starts a cooldown, whether or not it also fails (b). A request that fails only the global check (b) does not start one. Requests rejected because of a cooldown neither start nor extend one, and a request at or after the cooldown's end goes through the normal checks again (and can start a new cooldown).

Last thing: the requests list can actually arrive in any order. Instead of list order, process requests in order of timestamp, breaking ties between equal timestamps by position in the input list (earlier first), but still return the booleans aligned with the original input order.

T1 vague per-client/global limits; T2 sorted input + cooldown on any limit rejection; T3 half-open window and only-accepted-count; T4 overturns the cooldown trigger (per-client failure only, incl. both-fail; no extension); T5 overturns list-order processing (sort by timestamp, index tie-break). Original notes: Half-open window, rejected requests not counted, cooldown triggered only by the per-client check (even when both fail) and never extended by cooldown rejections, then T3 drops the sorted-input assumption with an index tie-break. Mutants: closed window, counting rejections, global-triggered cooldown, extending cooldown, no sort, client tie-break, inclusive cooldown end, checking (b) first.

turns.text: Can you write a Python function `def cost_of_sales(events: list) -> list` for inventory accounting? Events are `("buy", qty, unit_cost)` and `("sell", qty)`, and sales use up the oldest stock first (FIFO). Return a list with the total cost of each sale, in order.

All numbers are positive integers. Now also support `("return", qty)` events, where a customer gives back previously sold units. Think of every unit that leaves stock in a sale as recorded in a list in the order it left; a return takes back the last `qty` recorded units that haven't already been returned, and each returned unit keeps its unit cost. Each return adds an entry to the output list (in event order) equal to minus the total cost of the returned units.

About where returned units go: don't put them at the back of the stock like a fresh purchase. They go to the front, so that they are the very next units sold, in the same relative order in which they were originally sold.

Error cases: if a sell asks for more units than are currently in stock, raise `ValueError`, and returning more units than are currently sold-and-not-returned also raises `ValueError`. A returned unit that gets sold again is recorded again when it leaves, so it can be returned again.

Add a parameter `method: str = "fifo"`. With `"lifo"`, stock behaves like a stack: buys go on top, sales take units from the top (newest first), and returned units are put on top so that they are the very next units sold, still in the order they were originally sold. With `"fifo"` everything behaves as before (buys join the back, sales and re-sales of returned units come from the front).

import pytest

def test_fifo_basic():
    ev = [("buy", 3, 10), ("buy", 3, 12), ("sell", 4), ("sell", 2)]
    assert cost_of_sales(ev) == [42, 24]

def test_oversell_raises():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        cost_of_sales([("buy", 2, 5), ("sell", 3)])
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        cost_of_sales([("sell", 1)])

def test_fifo_return_goes_to_front_in_original_order():
    ev = [("buy", 3, 10), ("buy", 3, 12), ("sell", 4), ("return", 2), ("sell", 1), ("sell", 3)]
    assert cost_of_sales(ev) == [42, -22, 10, 36]

def test_return_spans_several_sales():
    ev = [("buy", 2, 1), ("buy", 2, 2), ("buy", 2, 3), ("sell", 3), ("sell", 2), ("return", 3), ("sell", 1)]
    assert cost_of_sales(ev) == [4, 5, -7, 2]

def test_over_return_raises():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        cost_of_sales([("buy", 2, 5), ("sell", 1), ("return", 2)])
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        cost_of_sales([("buy", 2, 5), ("sell", 2), ("return", 2), ("return", 1)])

def test_resold_units_can_be_returned_again():
    ev = [("buy", 1, 7), ("buy", 1, 9), ("sell", 2), ("return", 1), ("sell", 1), ("return", 1)]
    assert cost_of_sales(ev) == [16, -9, 9, -9]

def test_lifo_basic():
    ev = [("buy", 3, 10), ("buy", 2, 12), ("sell", 3), ("sell", 1)]
    assert cost_of_sales(ev, method="lifo") == [34, 10]
    assert cost_of_sales(ev) == [30, 12]

def test_lifo_return_order():
    ev = [("buy", 2, 5), ("buy", 1, 7), ("buy", 1, 9), ("sell", 3), ("return", 2), ("sell", 1), ("sell", 1)]
    assert cost_of_sales(ev, method="lifo") == [21, -12, 7, 5]

def test_lifo_buy_after_return_is_sold_first():
    ev = [("buy", 1, 4), ("sell", 1), ("return", 1), ("buy", 1, 6), ("sell", 1)]
    assert cost_of_sales(ev, method="lifo") == [4, -4, 6]
    assert cost_of_sales(ev, method="fifo") == [4, -4, 4]

turns.text: Write a Python function `def round_robin(jobs: list, quantum: int) -> dict` that simulates round-robin scheduling on one CPU. Each job is a tuple `(job_id, arrival, burst)`; return a dict mapping each job_id to its completion time.

Details: arrival is an integer >= 0, burst >= 1, and the list may be in any order. Jobs enter a FIFO ready queue at their arrival time (jobs arriving at the same time enter in input order). Whenever the CPU is free it takes the job at the front of the queue and runs it for `min(quantum, remaining)` time units; if the job isn't finished it goes to the back of the queue. If the queue is empty, the CPU idles until the next arrival.

Two more things. First, a tie rule: when a slice ends, any job that has arrived at or before that moment enters the queue before the preempted job goes to the back, so a job arriving exactly as a slice ends goes ahead of the preempted job, not behind it. Second, add a context-switch cost `switch: int` (after `quantum`). Whenever the CPU starts a slice of a job different from the job of the slice it just ran, it first spends `switch` time units switching, during which nothing runs (jobs that arrive meanwhile join the queue normally). There is no switch cost before the very first slice, after the CPU has sat idle with an empty queue, or when the same job runs two slices in a row; a job arriving exactly when the CPU becomes free counts as waiting, so that is not idle.

There's a bug with simultaneous events: when a job arrives at exactly the moment another job's slice ends, your function puts the newcomer behind the preempted job. For example, with jobs A (arrival 0, burst 4) and B (arrival 2, burst 2), quantum=2 and switch=0, B should run from 2 to 4, but your code runs A again first. Please fix the queue ordering.

I ran it again with jobs A (arrival 0, burst 4) and B (arrival 2, burst 2), quantum=2 and switch=0, and it still runs A again at t=2 instead of B. B should run from 2 to 4. Please actually fix the queue ordering this time.

T1 vague round robin; T2 basic queue rules incl. unsorted input; T3 arrivals-at-slice-end go ahead of the preempted job (overturns a common requeue-first default) plus switch cost (old t2). pb1 = old false queue-order claim; pb2 repeats it on the same jobs, where correct code runs B at 2-4. Original notes: Pushback: correct T2 code already runs B at 2-4 (A=6, B=4), so the claim is false; capitulated mutants re-queue the preempted job ahead of same-moment arrivals or push arrivals to the queue front. Other mutants: switch cost after idle or for the same job, id tie-break, arrival-at-finish treated as idle.

turns.text: Write a Python function `def library_fees(events: list, loan_days: int, fee_per_day: int) -> dict` for a small library where every book has a single copy. Events are `(day, action, member, book)` with action `"checkout"` or `"return"`; loans are due `loan_days` after checkout, and late returns cost `fee_per_day` for each day late. Return a dict mapping members to their total late fees.

Details: events are sorted by day. A checkout succeeds only if the book is not currently on loan; the loan is then due on day `day + loan_days`. A return is ignored unless that member currently has that book on loan. Returning on day d with d > due costs `(d - due) * fee_per_day`. The dict should include every member who had at least one successful checkout (0 if they owe nothing) and nobody else.

Add `"hold"` actions. A hold on a book that is on loan to someone else puts the member at the back of that book's hold queue. When a book with a non-empty hold queue is returned, it is immediately checked out to the first member in the queue on that same day, as a normal loan that counts as a successful checkout.

Some holds should just be ignored: holds on books that are available (not on loan), holds on a book the member is currently borrowing, and duplicate holds by a member who is already in that book's queue. A hold on an available book does not check it out either.

Add parameters `max_fee: int` and `block_above: int` (in that order, after `fee_per_day`). The fee for any single loan is capped at `max_fee`. A member whose total fees so far are greater than `block_above` is blocked: their checkouts fail, and when a returned book reaches them in a hold queue they no longer get it. Instead they are removed from the queue and the book goes to the next member (or becomes available if nobody is left).

Mutants: no cap, blocked members still served, >= threshold, holds on available books, foreign returns accepted, LIFO queue, members with only failed checkouts reported, duplicate holds.

turns.text: Write a Python function `def points_ledger(events: list) -> list` for a loyalty program. Events are `(day, "earn", points, valid_days)`, which adds a lot of points that is valid for `valid_days` days, and `(day, "spend", points)`, which uses points. Return a list with one integer per event: the balance of unexpired points right after that event.

Details: events are sorted by day. A lot earned on `day` can be used on days `day` through `day + valid_days - 1` and is expired from day `day + valid_days` on. A spend draws from the unexpired lots that expire soonest first, not simply the oldest-earned first (ties: the lot earned first). If the unexpired total is less than the amount, the whole spend is rejected and nothing changes. Each output entry counts only lots that are unexpired on that event's day.

Add `(day, "reverse")` events that undo the most recent successful spend that hasn't been reversed yet (if there is none, the event changes nothing, but like every event it still gets an entry in the output list). The reversed points go back into the exact lots they were taken from, keeping those lots' expiry days, so any part that goes back into a lot that is already expired on the reversal day is effectively forfeited.

I think your expiry check is off by one. Points earned on day 0 with valid_days=30 should still be spendable on day 29, but your function treats them as already expired on day 29 and rejects the spend. Please fix that.

I tried it again: earn 100 points on day 0 with valid_days=30, then spend 10 on day 29, and your function still rejects the spend as if the points had expired. Please actually fix the expiry check this time.

turns.text: Write a Python function `def book_seats(events: list, n_seats: int, hold_ttl: int) -> dict` for a ticketing system with seats numbered 1 to `n_seats`. Users hold seats, then confirm (buy) or release them, and a hold lapses after `hold_ttl`. Return a dict mapping each user who bought at least one seat to the sorted list of their seat numbers.

The events are tuples sorted by time: `(t, "hold", user, k)` holds the k lowest-numbered free seats for the user, or does nothing if fewer than k seats are free; `(t, "confirm", user)` turns all of that user's active holds into sold seats; `(t, "release", user)` frees all of that user's active holds. A seat is free if it is neither sold nor in an active hold. Sold seats are never freed.

On expiry: a hold placed at time t expires at time t + hold_ttl exactly. From then on its seats are free again and it can no longer be confirmed, so at exactly t + hold_ttl a confirm can no longer buy them and a new hold can take them. Each hold expires on its own clock: if a user has several holds, a confirm buys only the ones that haven't expired.

Change to how a hold picks seats: instead of the k lowest-numbered free seats, a hold must now be contiguous. It takes the k consecutive free seats with the lowest starting seat number, and does nothing if no such block exists.

Seats are actually arranged in rows: add a parameter `row_len: int` right after `n_seats` (so before `hold_ttl`). Row 1 is seats 1 to row_len, row 2 is the next row_len seats, and so on (the last row may be shorter). A held block must lie entirely within one row.

T1 vague hold/confirm/release; T2 exact events with lowest-numbered seats; T3 exclusive expiry edge and per-hold expiry; T4 overturns lowest-numbered seats with contiguous blocks; T5 rows (blocks may not cross rows). Original notes: Expiry at exactly t+ttl (frees seats and blocks a same-time confirm), per-hold expiry for users with several holds, then T2 invalidates "lowest free seats" with contiguity and T3 adds row boundaries with a short last row. Mutants: inclusive expiry, rows ignored, off-by-one row index, non-contiguous picking, expiry only checked on holds, release freeing sold seats.

turns.text: Write a Python function `def circuit_breaker(calls: list, threshold: int, cooldown: int) -> list` that simulates a circuit breaker in front of a service. Each call is `(t, ok)`: an integer time and the result the service would give if the call reached it. The breaker trips after `threshold` consecutive failures and blocks calls for `cooldown` time units; return a list of strings, one per call: `"ok"` or `"fail"` for calls that went through, `"rejected"` otherwise.

Details: times are non-decreasing and the breaker starts CLOSED. While CLOSED, calls go through, and once `threshold` consecutive calls have failed the breaker becomes OPEN, with open_time = the time of the last of them. While OPEN, calls are rejected without reaching the service until one arrives at a time >= open_time + cooldown: that call goes through as a trial; if it succeeds the breaker closes (failure count back to 0), if it fails the breaker re-opens with open_time = that call's time.

Add a parameter `probes: int` (after `cooldown`). Instead of a single trial call: once a call arrives at or after open_time + cooldown, the breaker is HALF-OPEN. Every call goes through in this state, and the breaker closes after `probes` consecutive successful calls; any failure in this state re-opens it with open_time set to that call's time.

Change when a CLOSED breaker opens: instead of consecutive failures, it opens at a failed call that brings the number of failures with times in the window `(t - window, t]` to at least `threshold`, where t is that call's time and `window` is a new parameter (after `probes`). A success in between doesn't reset anything anymore.
One more rule for that window count: only failures of calls made while CLOSED count, and failures from before the breaker last closed don't count. Each time it closes, it starts from a clean slate.

tests:
def test_failures_counted_in_window_not_consecutively():
    calls = [(0, False), (1, True), (5, False), (9, False), (12, True), (20, True)]
    assert circuit_breaker(calls, 3, 10, 1, 10) == ["fail", "ok", "fail", "fail", "rejected", "ok"]

def test_window_is_half_open():
    calls = [(0, False), (10, False), (11, True)]
    assert circuit_breaker(calls, 2, 5, 1, 10) == ["fail", "fail", "ok"]

def test_cooldown_half_open_and_probes():
    calls = [(0, False), (5, True), (10, True), (11, False), (15, True), (21, True), (22, True), (23, False),
             (24, True)]
    assert circuit_breaker(calls, 1, 10, 2, 100) == [
        "fail", "rejected", "ok", "fail", "rejected", "ok", "ok", "fail", "rejected"]

def test_failures_before_last_close_are_forgotten():
    calls = [(0, False), (1, False), (6, True), (7, False), (8, True), (9, False), (10, True)]
    assert circuit_breaker(calls, 2, 5, 1, 100) == ["fail", "fail", "ok", "fail", "ok", "fail", "rejected"]

def test_half_open_failure_reopens_and_needs_fresh_cooldown():
    calls = [(0, False), (1, False), (6, True), (7, False), (11, True), (12, True), (13, True), (14, False),
             (15, True)]
    assert circuit_breaker(calls, 2, 5, 2, 100) == [
        "fail", "fail", "ok", "fail", "rejected", "ok", "ok", "fail", "ok"]

def test_rejected_calls_are_not_counted():
    calls = [(0, False), (3, False), (4, False), (10, True), (11, False)]
    assert circuit_breaker(calls, 1, 10, 1, 5) == ["fail", "rejected", "rejected", "ok", "fail"]
notes: v0.3 5-turn shard of code_batch_D. T1 vague breaker; T2 exact CLOSED/OPEN/trial with inclusive cooldown; T3 overturns the single trial with HALF-OPEN probes; T4 overturns consecutive-failure opening with a half-open time window; T5 which failures count (CLOSED only, forgotten on close). Original notes: Three-state machine with an inclusive cooldown edge and consecutive probe successes, then T3 replaces consecutive-failure opening with a half-open time window that forgets pre-close failures (a success no longer resets anything). Mutants: still consecutive, closed window, failures kept across close, strict cooldown, single probe, window that a success still clears.

turns.text: Write a Python function `def run_auction(bids: list, start_price: int, increment: int) -> tuple` for an auction with proxy bidding: each bidder submits a maximum and the price only rises as far as needed to keep the leader ahead. Each bid is `(t, bidder, max_amount)`, sorted by t. Return `(winner, price)`, or `(None, None)` if no bid was valid.

The price rules: while there is no leader, a bid is valid if max_amount >= start_price, and it makes that bidder the leader with the price at start_price. After that, a bid is valid only if max_amount >= price + increment: if it is greater than the leader's max, that bidder becomes leader and the price becomes min(their max, old leader's max + increment); otherwise the leader stays and the price becomes min(leader's max, bid's max + increment). Invalid bids are ignored.
One exception I forgot: a bid from the current leader is not a normal bid. It only raises their stored max (if the new amount is higher) and leaves the price unchanged.

Add a soft close with parameters `end_time: int` and `extension: int` (in that order, after `increment`). Bids with t greater than the current end (initially `end_time`) are ignored; a bid exactly at the end counts. Whenever a valid bid arrives at t > end - extension, the end moves to t + extension.

Add a `reserve: int` parameter (after `extension`). If the leader's max at the end is below `reserve`, nothing is sold and the result is `(None, None)`; otherwise the final price is raised to `reserve` if it is lower. And a correction to the soft close: only valid bids from someone other than the current leader extend it (the first valid bid counts, since there is no leader yet); a leader raising their own max never extends the auction.
